messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Name Reminders: Hearing related names
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kiet Pham is a forty-year-old Vietnamese-American journalist, currently divorced and living alone in a one-bedroom apartment in Houston. He came to the clinic after his editor placed him on indefinite leave, citing erratic behaviour and missed deadlines — a professional collapse that, in his own words, "finally made it impossible to pretend I was functioning."

Approximately fourteen months ago, Kiet was detained while reporting on labour conditions in a Southeast Asian country he had visited on assignment. Over the course of several days he was subjected to systematic physical and psychological torture by state security personnel. He was kept in a windowless room, deprived of sleep, beaten repeatedly, and at one point restrained while the muffled cries of children — detainees in an adjacent cell — filtered through the concrete wall. His captors used his full name with deliberate, almost ceremonial precision each time they addressed him before inflicting pain, so that the syllables of his own name became inseparable from what followed. There were periods he cannot account for at all: stretches of time that exist in his memory only as absence, bordered by images so extreme — the texture of a drain cover against his cheek, a guard's boot — that he has sometimes struggled to believe they happened to him rather than to someone he once interviewed.

When Kiet returned to the United States, the symptoms began quietly and then gathered force. The most immediate and destabilising triggers were sounds: a child crying in a supermarket aisle, the dizzy, nauseating lurch that arrived without warning in his inner ear, or hearing his own name — or names phonetically close to it — spoken aloud in an ordinary conversation. Each of these sensations pulled him back toward the memory with a violence that felt physical, and as they did, the fragmentary, gap-ridden quality of what he could recall made the intrusions worse rather than better. He could not deliberately reconstruct the sequence of events in any coherent way — the memory resisted orderly retrieval — and this incompleteness meant that when a trigger struck, what surfaced was not narrative but sensation: raw, contextless, and without edges. The gaps in his memory, rather than offering relief, left him in a state of chronic unresolved arousal, as though the story could not be filed because it had no ending he could access.

His appraisals of himself darkened steadily across the months following his return. He had come to believe, with a certainty he found difficult to articulate but impossible to dismiss, that something was fundamentally broken in him — not wounded, but defective, as though the events had revealed a flaw that had always been there. He was certain that people on the street could see it simply by looking at him, that his face or his bearing broadcast what had been done to him and, worse, what he believed he had allowed. He had acted in ways during his captivity that violated his own sense of who he was — he could not be more specific than that in session, and the memory gaps made precision impossible — and the shame this produced was not situational but ontological. These appraisals fed directly back into his sensitivity to triggers: hearing his name spoken casually by a colleague felt unbearable precisely because he believed the name now carried the mark of what he was. The shame also intensified his hypervigilance; convinced that others could read his degradation, he watched people's faces and body language with exhausting attention, scanning for signs of contempt or threat, which in turn kept his nervous system in a state of perpetual alarm and made ordinary sounds — a door slamming, a laugh in the corridor — land like blows.

The strategies Kiet developed to manage this state became, over time, their own form of damage. He stopped seeing the colleagues and friends he had known before the assignment, telling himself he could not bear for them to witness whatever they would inevitably see in him. He began eating less and less, not from appetite loss alone but as a form of control — one of the few domains in which he felt any agency — and the physical depletion this produced worsened his dizziness, which was itself a trigger, creating a loop he recognised intellectually but could not interrupt. He spent long hours at his desk not writing but replaying the lead-up to his detention, dwelling on every decision point, every moment at which he might have left earlier or filed differently or said something different to his fixer. This rumination, which felt like problem-solving, kept the traumatic material active and close, so that the threshold for the next intrusion lowered further. His withdrawal from social contact meant there was no one to interrupt the cycle, no relational friction to pull him back into ordinary time. His editor's call came after he submitted a piece that made no coherent sense — he had not noticed.

What Kiet most fears, sitting in the waiting room of this clinic, is that the defectiveness he feels is the accurate account of himself, and that therapy will confirm rather than challenge it. What he most hopes, though he has not yet said this aloud, is that someone will help him find the parts of the story he cannot remember — not because he wants to relive them, but because he has come to believe, quietly and desperately, that he cannot be a whole person until the gaps are filled.
